Scale Up, Scale Out Challenges Amplified For Clusters

2

Shares

Compute clusters offer more processing capacity but at the cost of higher power. Software is needed to allocate resources effectively and optimize networking and memory.

August 5th, 2026 -

By: Liz Allan

Key Takeaways:

Software can identify the efficient way for clusters to use hardware such as GPUs, then optimize the output against the power consumption.
The CPU is playing a larger role in the shift from AI training to inference. While this reduces GPU workloads, it places more pressure on memory speeds.
Agentic AI workflows and a mixture of expert models are driving innovations around the ability to keep the KV cache in the larger memory when the agent is not active, then push it back to the accelerator memory when it’s active.

Experts At The Table: Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss changes in AI data center architectures with Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at Arm; Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise; Moshiko Emmer, distinguished engineer at Cadence; Sharad Chole, chief scientist at Expedera; Cameron Brunner, head of HPC development at Siemens EDA; and Sumit Vishwakarma, director of strategic marketing at Synopsys. What follows are excerpts of that discussion. This is part 2 of a 3-part series. Read part one here.

L-R: Arm’s Bhattacharjee; Axiomise’s Darbari; Cadence’s Emmer; Expedera’s Chole; Siemens EDA’s Brunner; Synopsys’ Vishwakarma.
SE: Compared to the scale up and scale out of racks in a data center, can clusters help reduce power consumption, or do they use more power and are therefore a part of the AI data center’s power problem? Where do clusters sit in the landscape, and what role does software play?
Vishwakarma: You can think of it more like [power consumption] is a growing problem with clusters. That is where it would sit.
Brunner: We’re seeing customers that have racks, and they can’t actually run all their GPUs at full power. They don’t have enough power capacity to run them at full power. A very common thing that we’re working on right now to manage this power usage is identifying power at light [loads], so running GPUs at not max power and looking at the performance you can get out of it. Maybe you can run it at 50%, but it doesn’t double the time it takes, and you get better power per performance. They talk about power per token. Trying to use the software to identify the efficient way to use the hardware can help optimize the output against the power consumption, and that kind of intelligent cluster middleware can drive that type of utilization versus you just throwing all your applications down a machine and saying, ‘Use everything.’
Chole: If I categorize a cluster as a set of nodes that are co-located or connected in some special way, rather than just connected to the typical data center networking, then this problem becomes about whether there is a benefit to using a cluster topology rather than using a general cloud topology. The applications that can benefit from either scale-up or scale-out applications that are getting bottlenecked by just staying under a single server are the ones that get the benefit of going and using clusters as a whole. HPC AI is a typical use case. You can even have database systems that are close to the storage systems, and they are serving them through some sort of APIs. Another example is financial systems that have to do very low-latency prediction, so they are much more amenable to having a very dedicated connectivity, and uptime also needs to be very high. This gives some reason to actually build the clusters. I also want to separate the software clustering effort from the hardware clustering effort, because what we are doing on hardware clusters is basically connecting nodes in a way where there is a predefined topology. You have to reconfigure or rewire the data center again to be able to change that. But the software allocation and utilization of those pieces, or the slicing of that hardware cluster into software or virtual groups, is a different problem.
SE: With power trade-offs, where operators might say, ‘We’re not going to run the GPU at max,’ how do they calculate how much to push the GPU?
Brunner: In terms of the application, how you partition and monitor the hardware, and how you’re running your applications, provides a lot of additional value. To solve the [power] problem we just discussed, you need to know and see the history of previous workloads at run time. You need to monitor how work has been going through the system, and you’ll see through your results — you can do experiments on your cluster with your workloads — what the best outcomes would be. This is also a place where artificial intelligence, plugged into the metrics and the control of the HPC system, can really start automating a lot of this process, and it’s something Nvidia is really big on: power control. You can even identify different power performance profiles that you see per individual GPUs in a given cluster, so being able to steer workloads to specific machines that have different performance profiles is a feasible thing. I think AI will help really enable some of that automation. Right now, a human can do it with the tools that we have. It’s a little more work with more manual experimentation.
Bhattacharjee: Power is becoming the bottleneck now. Initially, it was the GPU availability and the like, but now it is coming down to power. There are a lot of interesting innovations going on to make sure that the power consumed is at a reasonable limit, by which you can scale. What we are seeing is that instead of having just GPUs do all the work, there is now a close orchestration between the CPU and the GPU in the system, and people are realizing that as you move from training to inference, the workload pattern is completely different. Training is all about crunching numbers — matrix multiplications across those several cores that are running on the GPU, and they are running at the highest frequency to get the best training outcome. However, if you go to inference, especially now with the agents coming in, agents are supposed to do people’s work at a much faster cadence. They are booking Uber rides for you, or booking flights for you, or doing some research. Those are not matrix multiplication and crunching number tasks. Those run very well on CPUs. What we are seeing is that there are a lot of workloads that are now running on CPUs, and when they’re running on CPUs, the GPUs can be at a lower power, and the CPUs are basically taking the workload hit, and they’re running it at a much lower power compared to the GPUs. Once they’re done, they hand it over to the accelerators for a certain portion where there is some reasoning work required, which does need an accelerator, so the GPU or a custom accelerator does the work at that time.
The GPU is the one that is taking the power, so there’s close power coordination as the workload shifts from the CPU to the GPU. A good example is what Nvidia has done with Grace Hopper or Vera Rubin. There are a lot of innovations happening to create an equivalent system to scale this across, because you can’t rely on one company to do everything. It’s going to go along a similar paradigm to where the CPU and GPUs work together, and now you can think about scaling it up across the rack and scaling out across multiple of those. The CPU has started taking a very central role in terms of how these workloads are being served, especially as the shift is happening from training to inference. Inference, as far as our understanding goes, is going to be +80% of the AI workloads going forward, as the models are getting more measured, so the training is at a stage where people are saying, ‘These are great for deployment,’ and as soon as you deploy, it’s all inference.
Brunner: It’s really important to talk about that transition from training to inference, and also the types of use cases that we’re asking the cluster to do. An inference workload is likely real-time, where somebody is waiting for that response. The training workload is more like a batch workload. Let’s say you’ve got eight hours. You submit it at night because it needs to be done when you get into work the next day. We can run at lower power over the evening, whereas we’re maybe always running inference at higher power. It’s another way of looking at using categories of the types of workloads that you’re running and the time you expect to get out of them, in terms of how you might want to steer power consumption.
Emmer: Clusters don’t solve the power problem by themselves. They can actually magnify it if the architecture causes too much data movement. The win comes when we use architectural specialization intelligently — CPU for control and orchestration, accelerators for dense math, local memory for hot data, and the interconnect only for traffic that truly needs to escape the node. So the metric I’d focus on is not raw power, but useful work per joule across the full hierarchy, or performance-per-watt.
SE: When it comes to interconnects, I/Os, and data flow, are there different challenges between rack scale up, scale out, and compute clusters, or are they similar?
Darbari: A cluster changes the design problem from building a powerful machine to engineering a coordinated distributed system. In a single server, the main concerns are typically local compute, memory, and I/O balance. In a cluster, performance depends heavily on workload partitioning, communication patterns, and whether the interconnect can carry synchronization and data movement efficiently.
Vishwakarma: The architect needs to think about the cluster as one unit and not just design the silicon for that specific package, so networking is the biggest bottleneck. You are as fast as your slowest network switch. Think about how fast the workloads are changing. As we’re doing more inferencing, it is not like training where I’m looking for one big compute, and nobody is interrupting me. Inferencing is when somebody is waiting for the response. You give a query to your GPT or any other model, and you’re expecting it to come back, and then you query another. There’s so much traffic going in, so the network problem and latency specifically have ballooned with the new workloads. What needs to be addressed is that you want the lowest latency for the traffic, not only within the chip. And the chip itself is evolving. Now the chip is not just a single die. It is a multi-die chip with two dies that talk to each other. There are 3D-ICs. So the signals are traveling from between the dies, all the way to the signals traversing between two nodes. Everything adds to the latency. We are looking at this problem of die-to-die communication, where we have the UCIe kind of IPs for the fast data communication, all the way to Ethernet and UALink for cross communication between the nodes.
SE: How does the memory usage change for clusters compared to racks?
Bhattacharjee: The problem that we are trying to solve is how to execute the workload at the lowest latency possible. If you look at the CPUs and the GPUs, they are usually inside the server. Today, the typical form factor is two CPUs connected to eight GPUs — that’s a sweet form factor. This might change in the future, to have different ratios, but if you look at the CPUs and break them down, the CPU has the fastest memory, which is L2 cache. Nowadays, you have CPUs with hundreds of cores, and each core has a dedicated L2 cache attached to it, which is the fastest cache that it can access. These are in nanoseconds. Whatever job it can do by holding things in this L2 cache, that’s what it’ll do, but it’s usually small in size, because it’s per core, typically in the one to two megabyte range. Then you have shared L3 cache, which is shared across all the cores. Let’s say a CPU has 128 cores, then all the 128 cores can now access the shared cache, and that shared cache is also typically one to two megabytes per core. If there are 128 cores, you have 128 megabytes of cache. It’s still small. We’re still talking about megabytes, but it’s some of the fastest access that the cores have now.
If you go out, and you have the DDR or the main memory attached, that’s much bigger. The DDRs are typically in the gigabyte range, so, depending on what the CPU supports, if it’s 12 DDR, you are now talking about tons of gigabytes of memory that is attached. That’s going to be slower compared to the caches, but much faster. Now we are talking about the millisecond range. Then there’s a link between the CPU and the GPU, and you want to make sure that the CPU can push the traffic as fast as possible to the accelerator for processing, and that’s where the link comes in.
Nvidia has done a good job in coming up with NVLink, which allows it to push traffic at a much faster cadence over the physical link. There’s a physical limit, of course. It’s done with the PCIe connection, and that has some limits, but they are doing interesting stuff using AMBA CHI, which is an open standard to move the traffic. As Sumit mentioned, there’s an industry-wide initiative to make that a standard, so that all the different CPUs and all the different accelerators can take a similar kind of speed-up approach. Then, if you go to the accelerator part, HBM (high bandwidth memory) is super fast, and that’s what the GPUs and accelerators normally use to process the traffic. But, again, it’s smaller in size, and it’s very expensive, so interesting innovations are going on, especially for a swarm of agents with multiple models in a mixture of experts (MoE), where you have multiple models doing different work, and one is handing over tasks to another. Can you now keep some of these contexts, which are called KV cache, in the larger memory when the agent is not active, and then push them back to the accelerator memory when it’s active? There’s a lot of innovation going on the software side to ensure that the system-level efficiency comes in. This is a huge topic. When you’re talking about efficiency at a cluster level, it’s a combination of software, hardware, interconnects, cache, and memory; all of that comes together, and then there is the networking aspect as well.
Brunner: That’s the big challenge when you go from one machine. It’s such a great breakdown of all of the challenges in a single machine, so it becomes another whole set of challenges, and another whole set of technology to start linking the machines together. There have been a lot of strategies with that over time. We have our low-latency networks — the big, common ones are (HPE) Slingshot and InfiniBand (from Mellanox, acquired by Nvidia). Then it’s a case of, how do you hook up a large number of machines? It’s kind of a simple problem. Get an InfiniBand switch and put it on a rack, plug in all the machines, and then all those machines are pretty quickly connected via their interconnect. Well, let’s say you have 500 racks. There isn’t a 500-port switch. How do you put all the racks together so you don’t incorporate bottlenecks? HPE has a strategy called Dragonfly Network Topology, which kind of tries to maximize utilization of the interconnect, so you don’t put bottlenecks in when you have a large collaborative job over a lot of machines in the environment. Because what they found was that the original type of strategies is hierarchical, where you would have a rack with all of its nodes, another rack with all of its nodes, and then let’s trunk those racks together. But now if you have a job that’s split between two racks, it saturates that connection and everything goes away, so this is a big, a big challenge.
Emmer: The biggest mistake is to think that scale-up and scale-out are just the same problem at different sizes. They’re different latency and bandwidth regimes. Scale-up is about preserving locality and reducing serialization/deserialization overhead. Scale-out is about minimizing synchronization penalties and containing traffic amplification. Inside the package, I can design for extremely high bandwidth and fine-grain communication. Across a node, I’m already paying a different cost. Across racks, the system must become much more selective about what traffic is truly latency critical. So architectural efficiency comes from keeping the right data local: weights, activations, KV cache, metadata, and control traffic. And only exporting what must move. At the cluster scale, performance is often determined less by peak compute and more by where the data is forced to travel.
Darbari: For a chip architect, the lower‑layer links matter because their bandwidth, latency, ordering guarantees, and failure behavior shape what the higher layers can realistically deliver. Above that come node-level fabrics and then inter-node networking across the wider cluster. Correctness becomes harder as well. A server is one tightly coupled failure domain, while a cluster consists of many independent components that can fail, restart, or become unreachable while the overall service continues running. That means architects must think in terms of protocols, distributed state, and recovery semantics rather than only local functional behavior.
